items.summary: The decision of Rajasthan High Court acting Chief Justice Sanjeev Prakash Sharma to stop holding court was not the consequence of any intervention by or direction from the Supreme Court but was a voluntary decision taken by the judge himself in view of the controversy over his continuance as the acting Chief Justice. Sources aware of the developments confirmed to Bar & Bench that Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant received a communication sent by Justice Sharma to the Supreme Court administration. The CJI was holding court on Monday when Justice Sharma's communication reached the Registrar General of the Supreme Court. The CJI was apprised of the communication only after he returned to his chambers following court proceedings. In his communication, Justice Sharma conveyed that he was voluntarily stepping away from holding court in view of the controversy. The development came amid protests at the Rajasthan High Court with lawyers resorting to strike against Justice Sharma, demanding that he be divested of his charge as the acting Chief Justice and that a permanent Chief Justice be appointed to the High Court. items.title: Exclusive: Supreme Court Collegium recommends Justice Sanjay K Agrawal as Rajasthan High Court Chief Justice
items.summary: The Supreme Court Collegium has recommended the appointment of Justice Sanjay K Agrawal of the Chhattisgarh High Court as the Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court, Bar & Bench has learnt. Significantly, the Collegium has also proposed that Justice Agrawal be immediately transferred to the Rajasthan High Court, pending his appointment as its Chief Justice. The move would mean that even if the process for his appointment as Chief Justice takes time, Justice Agrawal would join the Rajasthan High Court as its senior-most judge. Justice Agrawal is presently a judge of the Chhattisgarh High Court. He was elevated as an additional judge of that Court in September 2013 and made a permanent judge in March 2016. Before his elevation, he had served as the Advocate General of Chhattisgarh. The development assumes significance in the backdrop of the controversy surrounding the present acting Chief Justice of the Rajasthan High Court, Justice Sanjeev Prakash Sharma . items.summary: The Delhi High Court recently observed that the apprehension that homeless persons will be excluded from the draft electoral roll published after the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) in the national capital appeared to be without any basis. A Division Bench of Chief Justice Devendra Kumar Upadhyaya and Justice Tejas Karia made the observation while dismissing a public interest litigation (PIL) petition seeking directions to the Election Commission of India (ECI) to establish a special facilitative mechanism for homeless persons and those displaced by demolition drives. "Having considered the submissions on behalf of learned Senior Counsel for the petitioner as well as learned Counsel for the ECI, we are of the considered opinion that the Manual already provide process for determination of the ordinary residence in accordance with the Representation of People Act for homeless persons as per Clause 8.5 of the Manual. Therefore, the apprehension of the petitioner that the homeless persons shall be excluded from the Draft Electoral Roll appears to be without any basis," the Court said. items.title: Reclaiming the field: Mineral taxation, federalism and the MMDR (Amendment) Act 2026
items.summary: The Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Amendment Act, 2026 (the “ 2026 Act ”/” Act ”) introduces a significant shift in the fiscal framework governing India’s mineral sector. Coming shortly after the Supreme Court’s nine-judge Bench decision in Mineral Area Development Authority v. Steel Authority of India, (2024) 10 SCC 1 (MADA), the amendment seeks to clarify and, in important respects, reshape the limits within which States may impose levies connected with mineral rights and mineral-bearing land. The resulting questions of legislative competence, federalism and retrospectivity are likely to be closely tested before the courts. The amendment is the latest in a series of changes to India’s mineral regulatory framework. The 2015 amendment introduced auctions; the 2021 amendment liberalised captive production; and the 2023 and 2025 amendments opened critical minerals to greater private participation. The 2026 Act takes the next step by seeking to establish a more uniform fiscal framework for mineral development. Its significance, however, extends beyond taxation: it raises broader questions about the constitutional balance between Union regulation and State taxing power

items.title: Supreme Court Collegium recommends Justice AY Kogje as Chief Justice of Madhya Pradesh High Court
items.summary: Justice Alpesh Yeshvant Kogje from Gujarat High Court has been recommended for appointment as the Chief Justice of the Madhya Pradesh High Court. The recommendation was made by the Supreme Court Collegium in its meeting held on August 31. Justice Kogje is presently serving as a judge of the Gujarat High Court. Justice Kogje completed his B.Sc. in Chemistry in 1990 and earned his law degree from the Faculty of Law at Maharaja Sayajirao University of Baroda in 1993. He joined the Bar in 1993. Throughout his career as counsel, he held several significant roles, including Additional Public Prosecutor from 2002 to 2007, Standing Counsel for the Central Excise and Customs Department, and Special Public Prosecutor for the Special Investigation Team (SIT), where he notably handled a large volume of important cases arising from the 2002 Godhra riots. He was elevated as an additional judge of the Gujarat High Court in April 2016. He was subsequently appointed as a permanent judge of the Gujarat High Court in March 2018. The Madhya Pradesh High Court is presently functioning with 38 judges while its sanctioned strength is 53. [Read Collegium Statement]
